<explanation>
Based on our analysis of the project file tree and README, here are detailed instructions for drawing an accurate system design diagram for git-who:

1. Project Overview and Main Purpose:
   • git-who is a command‐line tool written primarily in Go that analyzes a Git repository’s commit history to show which authors are mainly responsible for components of a codebase. Its subcommands (table, tree, hist) let users view contributions using different metrics.
   • The project is structured as a monolithic command-line application with well-modularized internal packages to handle caching, Git integration, concurrent processing, formatting, and tallying statistics.

2. Identify the Major Components:
   • CLI Frontend & Entry Point: 
     – Represented by files such as main.go, cache.go, dump.go, hist.go, and parse.go.
     – This layer handles command parsing (subcommands like table, tree, hist) and user input.
   • Git Integration Module:
     – Found under the internal/git package. This component is responsible for wrapping Git commands, parsing output, and managing commit history extraction.
   • Caching Layer:
     – The internal/cache package (and its backends like gob.go, json.go, noop.go) encapsulates caching functionality, storing parsed Git data on a per-repository basis.
   • Concurrency Management:
     – Directory internal/concurrent shows components for executing tasks in parallel (e.g., worker.go) to efficiently process large commit histories.
   • Tally and Analysis:
     – The internal/tally package computes statistics on commits, file counts, and line modifications that drive the “table” and “hist” views.
   • Output Formatting and Presentation:
     – internal/format and internal/pretty handle formatting of tables, trees, and timelines, ensuring the CLI output is user-friendly.
   • Utility Functions:
     – internal/utils (with flagutils, iterutils, timeutils) provides helper functions for parsing command-line flags, iterating over collections, and timestamp management.
   • Docker Container Wrapper:
     – The docker directory (including Dockerfile) shows that the project is also distributed (and run) in a containerized environment.
   • Build and Test Support:
     – Files like Rakefile and the test-repo directory indicate that there is an external build/test orchestration (using Ruby Rake for source builds) and a submodule for repository tests.

3. Relationships and Data Flow:
   • The CLI Frontend (main.go) receives user commands and routes them to the appropriate subcommand handler.
   • Depending on the subcommand invoked, it then calls the Git Integration Module:
       - For example, when a user runs “git who table”, the CLI layer invokes functions in internal/git to extract commit history.
   • The retrieved data are then optionally cached (using the caching component) so that repeated queries are faster.
   • Concurrent modules (internal/concurrent) are used to process commit data and run tasks in parallel – for instance, concurrently analyzing several paths in a repository.
   • The tally module aggregates the results (commit counts, file modifications, line changes) and passes these metrics to the formatting modules.
   • Formatting components (internal/format and internal/pretty) then prepare the final output (tables, trees, or histograms) which is printed to the console.
   • The Docker container (captured in the docker directory) encloses the entire application runtime when deployed using Docker commands.

4. Architectural Patterns and Design Principles:
   • Modularity: Each function is separated into its own subpackage (e.g., git, cache, concurrent, tally, format, pretty), abiding by single responsibility.
   • Separation of Concerns: There is a clear boundary between data gathering (Git integration), processing (concurrent tallying, caching), and presentation (formatting).
   • Concurrency: The design leverages Go’s concurrency model (seen in internal/concurrent) to process large datasets efficiently.
   • Extensibility: With clearly defined modular components, it’s straightforward to add new subcommands or update output formats.

5. Guidelines for Tailoring the Diagram:
   • Use a block diagram style where each major component is represented by a labeled rectangle. For example:
       - “CLI Frontend / Entry Point” (main.go, etc.)
       - “Git Integration” (internal/git)
       - “Caching Layer” (internal/cache & backends)
       - “Concurrency Manager” (internal/concurrent)
       - “Tally / Aggregation Engine” (internal/tally)
       - “Formatting & Presentation” (internal/format, internal/pretty)
       - “Utilities” (internal/utils)
       - “Testing & Build Infrastructure” (Rakefile, test-repo)
       - “Container Deployment” (docker)
   • Draw directional arrows to illustrate the flow:
       - CLI Frontend → Git Integration (for fetching commit data)
       - Git Integration → Caching Layer (for storing/fetching parsed history)
       - Git Integration, Caching → Concurrency Manager (parallel processing)
       - Concurrency Manager → Tally Engine (aggregation of contributions)
       - Tally Engine → Formatting & Presentation (prepare output)
       - Finally, output is rendered back to the CLI.
   • Use color coding or distinct shapes to highlight, for instance, core logic components vs. auxiliary functionalities (e.g., use one color for internal processing modules and another for infrastructure / deployment components like Docker).

6. Additional Instruction Details:
   • Clearly label each component with its package name (e.g., internal/git, internal/cache) and possible responsibilities.
   • Annotate arrows with short notes (like “fetch commit history”, “cache results”, “concurrent processing”, or “format output”).
   • Ensure components like the Docker container are shown as an outer boundary or separate context that encapsulates the application.
   • Optionally, note that build tooling (Rakefile) and Git submodules (test-repo) support development and testing workflows.
   • Emphasize that the diagram should be as detailed as possible—include subcomponents if necessary (for instance, under caching, show that there are multiple backends for different formats).

By following these instructions, you’ll create a comprehensive system design diagram that accurately maps the git-who project’s architecture – from the user command-line interface through processing and output formatting, along with the infrastructure considerations like caching, concurrency, and containerized deployment.

This detailed approach ensures that every crucial architectural element is captured and understood. Adjust the diagram’s granularity based on the audience’s familiarity with Go projects or similar CLI tools, but do not overcomplicate; the goal is to illustrate the clear flow from input to output through distinct, modular components.
</explanation>
